newsitem.title: UK: Morgan Grenfell acts to boost MGAM reputation.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Grenfell acts to boost MGAM reputation.

text.p: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell on Wednesday confirmed the sacrifice of four key managers in an attempt to restore faith in its troubled asset management group, still reeling from last month's revelations of misvaluations in three of its funds and the sacking of fund manager Peter Young.

The investment banking arm of Germany's mighty Deutsche Bank said Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) head Keith Percy would leave and be replaced by Robert Smith, head of development capital and the man chosen earlier to lead an internal investigation into what went wrong at the funds.

Percy, along with directors Glyn Owen, Graham Kane and Michael Wheatley will all leave the firm. Owen was MGAM's chief investment officer and Young's immediate boss, Wheatley was compliance director and Kane headed MGAM's unit trust business.

"Our internal investigations have revealed management failings which contributed to the problems in our unit trust business and these changes have been made as a result," DMG chief executive Michael Dobson said.
The departures follow revelations of major problems in three MGAM funds last month. The discovery of misvaluations of speculative unlisted stocks led to their temporary suspension.
Trading in the funds, which were held by around 90,000 retail investors, resumed after Deutsche Bank stepped in with a 180 million pound ($285 million) cash injection.

Young, who is currently being investigated by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO), has said he is not guilty of any criminal activity and is being made a scapegoat for failings. He was dismissed on the grounds of alleged "gross misconduct".

Some fund industry sources questioned whether the departures of the top managers, which they said were inevitable, would be enough given lingering questions over whether the trust business would be brought under stronger German control.
But by making top-level changes DMG had probably done enough "to get them back on track," one fund manager said.

A Deutsche spokesman in Frankfurt declined to comment on when Udo Behrenwaldt, a managing director of its German investment subsidiary DWS who was sent to London last month as an adviser to MGAM, would return. This was linked to a possible rerouting of management reporting lines to Frankfurt.

One banking source said a possibility was for the retail asset management portion of MGAM's 70 billion pounds ($111 billion) of funds under management to be moved to Frankfurt, leaving the institutional bulk under London's control.

Earlier DMG said a senior associate director, Paul Ebling, would also leave the firm. Apart from Smith, it did not name replacements for any of the managers and a spokesman told Reuters the decisions were up to the new management.

Smith said the internal inquiry was largely complete and MGAM would continue to work with Britain's investments watchdog, the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) and other regulators "to resolve outstanding issues".

IMRO is conducting its own investigation into the funds and is not expected to report on its findings for some months. If the regulator finds MGAM breached the rules, it could lead to hefty fines and possible action against individuals.
Smith reiterated a pledge that investors would not be left short-changed. "If compensation is found to be due under IMRO rules or other legislation, we will pay it," he said.

He said the priority was to restore MGAM's reputation in the unit trust business and said he was determined that MGAM would continue to deliver "superior performance for clients in virtually every asset class."
Deutsche Bank has said since the beginning of the debacle that those with immediate responsibility for Young's activities would not continue to work for the group.
Dobson paid tribute to the departing executives for their "major contribution to our asset management business over many years."
